latestPosts.caption:
We may be among the first generations of women in our families to truly understand our ADHD or neurodivergence.

But that doesn’t mean the generations before us weren’t living with similar challenges. They just didn’t have the language, awareness or support many of us are beginning to have today.

And I think this is where things can become quite uncomfortable.

Because once we understand our ADHD, our emotional needs and the ways we’ve learnt to cope, we may start looking at our family relationships differently.

The roles we’ve always played. The expectations we’ve accepted. The guilt we’ve carried. The responsibility we’ve felt for keeping everyone else happy.

And suddenly there’s a disconnect between what we now know we need as adults and the family dynamics we’ve been part of for decades.

In this clip, Kristen Carder, host of @i.have.adhd.podcast talks about what she believes could be the next stage of growth for the ADHD community.

Not just learning to manage our brains, but learning to build healthier, more authentic relationships.

And this isn’t about blaming previous generations or cutting family ties.

We can have compassion for the generations before us without continuing every pattern they passed down.

We can love people and still need boundaries. We can understand someone’s behaviour without having to accept it. And we can choose to relate and parent differently.

🎧 Kristen and I explore generational neurodivergence, family roles, guilt and boundaries in this week’s ADHD Women’s Wellbeing Podcast.

Comment PODCAST and I’ll send you the link to listen. 

I’d love to know: Has understanding your ADHD changed how you see your family relationships or how you parent your own children?

Share this with someone who might be navigating this part of their own journey.

EP 107 | ADHD Medication, Toxic Guilt and Self Compassion: You’re Not in Trouble for ADHDers with Kristen Carder

Are they mad at me?
Did I do something wrong?
Why do I always feel like I’m in trouble?

If you’re an ADHDer, you probably feel it in your body before you can even explain it.

This week I sat down with Kristen Carder @i.have.adhd.podcast, host of the I Have ADHD podcast and author of the brand new book You’re Not in Trouble.

We talked about:

 *The layer of relationships as an ADHDer

*Why Kristen believes ADHD is really a regulation disorder
 

*The medication myths she wishes everyone knew

*The difference between moral guilt and toxic guilt

*Why I now ask to see a budget before I lend money to anyone

*How self compassion stops one mistake from ruining your whole day

*The guilt that stops you saying no to people is often the same guilt that stops you saying no with your money.

One line from Kristen’s book ( You're not in trouble)  stayed with me: “You’re late, but you’re not in trouble.”

Comment 107 and I’ll send you the episode link.

latestPosts.caption:
Some conversations about ADHD go beyond understanding our brains and managing everyday life. They take us into the relationships, family dynamics and identity roles we may have carried since childhood.

My latest conversation with @i.have.adhd.podcast host, Kristen Carder, is one of those episodes.

It’s a conversation that might feel difficult to have, or even listen to, but I think many women will recognise parts of themselves in it, even if their experiences have been very different.

In this clip, Kristen shares findings from a survey she commissioned involving 2,165 adults with ADHD, exploring their childhood experiences of feeling misunderstood, walking on eggshells and learning to prioritise other people’s emotions over their own.

And sometimes, those patterns follow us into adulthood.

We become the peacekeepers, the people-pleasers, the ones who feel responsible for everyone else’s happiness. Saying no can bring up enormous guilt, even when we’re simply protecting our own wellbeing.

Importantly, this isn’t about blaming parents, cutting family ties or assuming every ADHD adult had a difficult childhood.

It’s about recognising where our boundaries may have been overlooked, pushed or taken advantage of, and understanding that we’re allowed to change those dynamics.

We can love our families, appreciate the circumstances they grew up in, and still acknowledge where our own needs haven’t been met.

Kristen and I explore emotionally immature family dynamics, generational neurodivergence, moral versus toxic guilt, and why building self-trust and healthier boundaries can be such an important part of understanding ourselves after a late ADHD diagnosis.

There may be parts that resonate deeply, others that don’t, and perhaps some that bring up feelings you haven’t had space to explore before.

Take what feels helpful and leave the rest. ❤️

🎧 Listen to my latest conversation with Kristen Carder on The ADHD Women’s Wellbeing Podcast.
